overview: This map label groups communities in southern and central Sweden between 800 and 1000. Here “Goths” is best understood as the Götar of southern Sweden, alongside the Svear, rather than as a reference to Italy’s or Spain’s Gothic kingdoms. The outline is a broad regional grouping, not a verified frontier of one continuously united state. Trading towns and royal centres developed amid communities with distinct regional identities.

periods.title: Regional communities and growing royal centres
periods.summary: This mapped interval includes Birka’s trading peak and the beginnings of Sigtuna.

items.text: Birka stood on Björkö in Lake Mälaren, where important waterways met. Across the water, Hovgården on Adelsö was a royal domain associated with governing the town. Harbour, defences and cemeteries survive as parts of the archaeological landscape. Between roughly 750 and 980, this small place connected its hinterland with long-distance commerce.

Inside Birka’s rampart, wooden houses crowded along narrow lanes. Smiths, jewellers working bronze and precious metals, and craftspeople shaping bone and horn made goods there. These workshops brought specialised skills together. The town’s importance depended on making and exchanging useful and attractive things as well as receiving travelling merchants.

Archaeological work places Sigtuna’s foundation in the 970s, during Erik the Victorious’s reign. Its principal street and division into blocks retain much of that early plan. The county museum describes it as a Christian community from its beginning. The stone church ruins visible today largely belong to later medieval development.

sections.title: Children, winter and a careful step

items.text: A child buried in Birka grave Bj 463 died at about five or six years old. A gilded brooch, glass beads, knife and bone needle case accompanied the burial. The child is usually called the Birka Girl, although the identification as female rests on the gifts rather than certainty from the skeleton. The costly objects suggest a wealthy family.

A horn duck and a tiny human foot carved in bone from Birka may have been toys. Small bronze bells found in children’s graves might have rattled during play, or served as protective amulets. Archaeologists can identify the materials and shapes more confidently than the precise games children invented with them.

Many bone skates have been found at Birka. Made from cattle or horse foot bones, they average about 20 centimetres long, suggesting use by children. Many have no holes for straps. Perhaps a skater simply stood on them and pushed along with an ice pole; alternatively, some examples may have been unfinished.

For ordinary winter walking, people could fasten iron spikes beneath their shoes with leather straps. Horses also received spikes. The museum connects these finds with the danger of slippery ground, while skeletons show that many broken bones healed. Staying upright mattered whether someone was carrying dinner or leading an animal.

Food residues in pots and preserved human waste give unusually direct clues to meals. The Swedish History Museum’s Viking-period synthesis describes oat and barley dishes, with sheep and cattle among the meat sources. Charred bread also survives, sometimes from graves. Ancient rubbish can answer a question that grand monuments cannot: what was for dinner?

A household’s spoons could be wood, horn or bone; a small iron knife cut bread or meat. Pots of clay, iron or soapstone stood on hot coals or hung over a fire. Wooden plates and cups usually rotted away. Waterlogged ground sometimes preserved this ordinary kitchen equipment, giving archaeologists a rare look inside the cupboard.

Combs, tweezers, ear-cleaning tools and washbasins show that personal care mattered. Some people even had glass mirrors. These finds complicate the familiar picture of an endlessly muddy Viking: hair and beards could be carefully maintained. They do not tell us how often every household washed, but they show the equipment people chose to keep.

The ninth-century Rök stone in Östergötland commemorates Vämod, the dead son of Varin. It preserves a family’s act of remembrance in runic writing. The monument belongs within this record’s period, earlier than the great wave of Swedish memorial stones around and after 1000. Its existence also gives southern Sweden a voice alongside Birka’s archaeological finds.

A silver coin struck at Sigtuna around 995 carries “ONLAF REX”, meaning “King Olaf”. This is Latin lettering and a Latin royal title, not a sample of ordinary spoken Swedish. The coin followed an English model for Olof Skötkonung, the first Swedish king to issue coins. The museum’s specimen was found in a hoard on Gotland.

ending.text: The map’s endpoint at 1000 does not mark the disappearance of these communities. Birka’s commercial role ended during the late tenth century, while Sigtuna developed as a royal and Christian centre. Regional populations continued within the changing institutions of medieval Sweden. The sources describe a shift in towns and authority, not a single documented conquest ending a “Swedes and Goths” state.
